doc.title: Abe Most interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 13, 1999

title: Big bands folding in 1946 and the Hickory House before going west
summary: Back from the Army he ran a quartet in New York, played the Hickory House, then headed west to Tommy Dorsey.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: 1946, a whole slew of big bands called it quits.
Did you see that coming as a sideman, and did it affect what you wanted to do, your choice of career at that point?

No. Because that’s when I joined Tommy Dorsey. 1945. I was out of the Army, I was in New York with a quartet like I described earlier, with the accordion, bass and drums. We tried to knock around Long Island, New York doing casuals. I wasn’t making any money and I paid the guys what I could, and it wasn’t happening. And then we had a little — the Hickory House. We had a chance to go in the Hickory House which I did. And then we did some more casuals. Now I had another chance to go in the Hickory House, but I was already practically packed and on my way to the coast and I figured to go through what I had already gone through just to stay at the Hickory House, which was — if that’s as far as I can go, I’d better go somewhere. So I came to the coast and wound up going with Tommy Dorsey. So that was the time I decided to make the move out and stay here. We stayed, I went with Tommy Dorsey and then back with Les and then into the studios.
